comment: Per-kind section specification for wiki entity notes. This file decides which headings a generator owns; the paired template in references/templates decides what a note looks like. doctor checks the two agree. 'guidance' is sent to the drafting model verbatim, so it is prompt text as much as configuration. Length budgets are first guesses and expected to be retuned once real runs land. The three species kinds carry a 'table' fill section, Phenology, whose rows are region-scoped: timing varies by latitude and elevation, so a window without a region is not a fact about anywhere. forge/lib/vault_phenology.py compiles those tables into an index the naturalist dashboard reads, and references/phenology-events.json is the controlled event vocabulary the columns refer to.

concept.lead_guidance: One or two sentences defining the idea. Say what it claims, not why it matters. No hedging, no 'refers to'.

sections.guidance: The definition. One or two sentences.

sections.heading: Key Points
sections.guidance: Three to five bullets: the moves the concept makes, what it argues against, where it does work. One claim per bullet, no bullet repeating the lead.

sections.heading: Origin
sections.guidance: One line: who introduced it, in what work, and when. Omit entirely rather than guessing a date.

sections.heading: Key Thinkers
sections.guidance: Names only, optionally with a three-word gloss. People who developed or contested the concept, not everyone who cited it.

sections.heading: Distinctions
sections.guidance: Where the concept is routinely misread, and what it is confused with. Include only a confusion the sources actually flag.

sections.heading: Sources
sections.guidance: Deterministic. Rendered from the archived sources, never written by the model.

sections.heading: Notes
sections.guidance: Owner-authored. Never written or read by the pipeline.
Deterministic. Rendered from the citations the draft actually used.

term.lead_guidance: One sentence that lets a reader use the term correctly. This is a glossary entry, not an essay.

sections.guidance: The definition, in one sentence. Expand an acronym on first use.

sections.heading: Usage
sections.guidance: One or two lines on where the term is used and by whom, including any field-specific narrowing of its meaning.

sections.heading: Origin
sections.guidance: One line: where the term comes from. Omit rather than guessing.

sections.heading: Sources
sections.guidance: Deterministic.

sections.heading: Notes
sections.guidance: Owner-authored.
Deterministic.

practice.lead_guidance: One or two sentences naming the practice and what doing it consists of.

sections.guidance: What the practice is and what performing it involves.

sections.heading: How It Works
sections.guidance: Three to five bullets describing the method as a practitioner would recognize it. Describe the technique, do not instruct the reader.

sections.heading: Origin
sections.guidance: One line: the tradition or lineage it comes from, and roughly when.

sections.heading: Key Thinkers
sections.guidance: People who codified or transmitted the practice.

sections.heading: Sources
sections.guidance: Deterministic.

sections.heading: Notes
sections.guidance: Owner-authored.
Deterministic.

figure.lead_guidance: One or two sentences: field, dates in parentheses, and the one thing they are known for. This is the single most useful line on the card and it is what every figure note currently lacks.

sections.guidance: Who they are: nationality or field, lifespan in parentheses when the sources give it, and what they are known for. Never invent a date; omit the parenthetical instead. For a living person, claim nothing the archived sources do not state.

sections.heading: Key Ideas
sections.guidance: Three to five bullets, each naming one idea and saying what it claims. Wikilink a concept only when that note already exists.

sections.heading: Key Works
sections.guidance: Format each as *Title* (year). Two to five entries, the works they are actually read for. Omit a year you cannot source.

sections.heading: Position
sections.guidance: One or two lines: the tradition they work in and what they argue against. Omit unless the sources make it clear.

sections.heading: Associated Concepts
sections.guidance: Deterministic. Rendered from the note's own related property, never written by the model.

sections.heading: Colleague Thinkers
sections.guidance: Deterministic. Rendered from the note's own related property, never written by the model.

sections.heading: Sources
sections.guidance: Deterministic.

sections.heading: Notes
sections.guidance: Owner-authored.
Deterministic.

work.lead_guidance: One or two sentences: author, year, form, and the work's central claim or premise.

sections.guidance: Author, year, and form, then the one-line thesis or premise. Omit a year you cannot source.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.guidance: Three to five bullets tracing what the work does, in its own order. Works for an argument, a narrative, or a track list alike.

sections.heading: Key Concepts
sections.guidance: Ideas this work is the standard citation for. Wikilink a concept only when that note already exists.

sections.heading: Sources
sections.guidance: Deterministic.

sections.heading: Notes
sections.guidance: Owner-authored.
Deterministic.

place.lead_guidance: One or two sentences: what and where it is.

sections.guidance: What the place is and where. Name the containing region so the note is locatable without a map.

sections.heading: Significance
sections.guidance: Two to four bullets on why the place recurs as a subject — historical, cultural, or personal.

sections.heading: Context
sections.guidance: One line of orienting detail: region, period, scale.

sections.heading: Sources
sections.guidance: Deterministic.

sections.heading: Notes
sections.guidance: Owner-authored.
Deterministic.

event.lead_guidance: One or two sentences: what happened, when, and where.

sections.guidance: What happened, with the date and place. Omit a date you cannot source rather than approximating it.

sections.heading: What Happened
sections.guidance: Three to five bullets in chronological order. Facts, not interpretation.

sections.heading: Significance
sections.guidance: One or two lines on what changed as a result.

sections.heading: Sources
sections.guidance: Deterministic.

sections.heading: Notes
sections.guidance: Owner-authored.
Deterministic.

animal.lead_guidance: One or two sentences: what the animal is, the family it belongs to, its range, and its size. Give the scientific name once, in italics, if the note title does not already carry it.

sections.guidance: What it is, where it lives, and how big it is. A reader should be able to picture it from this line alone.

sections.heading: Identification
sections.guidance: Three to five bullets naming what distinguishes this animal in the field: size, markings, silhouette, call, gait. Prefer a feature a person can check at a distance over one that needs the animal in hand.

sections.heading: Habitat & Range
sections.guidance: One or two lines: the habitat types it uses and the extent of its range. Name the continent or region rather than assuming the reader's.

sections.heading: Diet
sections.guidance: What it actually eats, and how that shifts across the year where the sources say so. Seasonal diet is what makes an animal findable.

sections.heading: Behavior
sections.guidance: Three to five bullets on how it lives: activity period, sociality, territory, denning or roosting, response to people. Describe what it does, do not instruct the reader.

sections.heading: Life Cycle
sections.guidance: Breeding system, gestation or incubation, litter or clutch size, how long young stay dependent, and typical lifespan. Durations belong here; the calendar months they fall in belong in Phenology.

sections.heading: Tracks & Sign
sections.guidance: What it leaves behind: track shape and size, scat, scratchings, nests, browse. Omit rather than guessing; a wrong track description sends someone after the wrong animal.

sections.heading: Phenology

columns.heading: Event
columns.guidance: One of the events named in phenology-events.json for this kind. Nothing else.

columns.heading: Window
columns.guidance: A month (Feb), a month range (Jan-Mar), or year-round. Never a specific date: a window is a pattern, not an appointment.

columns.heading: Region
columns.guidance: A [[wikilink]] to the region the window holds in, or global when the source states it range-wide. Never generalize one region's timing to another.

columns.heading: Basis
columns.guidance: sourced when a citation states it, inferred when you are reasoning from a stated fact. Never write observed: that value is reserved for the owner's own records.

sections.guidance: One row per event the sources actually give timing for, in calendar order. Timing varies by latitude and elevation, so a row without a region is worth less than no row at all: name the region the source describes, and omit the event entirely rather than transplanting a window from somewhere else. Prefer a coarse window you can support over a precise one you cannot. For an animal the events are present, arrival, departure, mating, birth, fledging, dispersal, moult, torpor, hibernation, and migration.

sections.heading: Conservation
sections.guidance: One line: the status a body such as the IUCN assigns, and the main pressure on it. Name the assessing body; a status without one is unciteable.

sections.heading: Sources
sections.guidance: Deterministic.

sections.heading: Notes
sections.guidance: Owner-authored.
Deterministic.

plant.lead_guidance: One or two sentences: what the plant is, its family, its growth form, and its range. Give the scientific name once, in italics, if the note title does not already carry it.

sections.guidance: Growth form, family, size at maturity, and where it grows. Say whether it is native to the region it is best known in.

sections.heading: Identification
sections.guidance: Leaf shape and arrangement, flower structure and colour, bark or stem, height, and anything that separates it from its obvious neighbours. Arrangement and margin distinguish more plants than colour does.

sections.heading: Habitat & Range
sections.guidance: One or two lines: soil, moisture, light, elevation, and the extent of its range. Say if it is introduced or invasive anywhere the sources name.

sections.heading: Life Cycle
sections.guidance: Annual, biennial or perennial; how it reproduces and spreads; how long to maturity; whether it is deciduous or evergreen. Durations here, calendar months in Phenology.

sections.heading: Ecology
sections.guidance: What depends on it: pollinators, the larvae it hosts, the animals that eat its fruit or browse it, what it associates with. This is the section that connects a plant note to the animal notes.

sections.heading: Phenology

columns.heading: Event
columns.guidance: One of the events named in phenology-events.json for this kind. Nothing else.

columns.heading: Window
columns.guidance: A month (Feb), a month range (Jan-Mar), or year-round. Never a specific date: a window is a pattern, not an appointment.

columns.heading: Region
columns.guidance: A [[wikilink]] to the region the window holds in, or global when the source states it range-wide. Never generalize one region's timing to another.

columns.heading: Basis
columns.guidance: sourced when a citation states it, inferred when you are reasoning from a stated fact. Never write observed: that value is reserved for the owner's own records.

sections.guidance: One row per event the sources actually give timing for, in calendar order. Timing varies by latitude and elevation, so a row without a region is worth less than no row at all: name the region the source describes, and omit the event entirely rather than transplanting a window from somewhere else. Prefer a coarse window you can support over a precise one you cannot. For a plant the events are leaf-out, bud-break, flowering, fruiting, seed-drop, senescence, and dormancy.

sections.heading: Uses & Cautions
sections.guidance: Owner-authored. Edibility, toxicity, and medicinal use are judgments a person makes with a field guide in hand and their own risk to carry, so the pipeline never writes or reads this section.

sections.heading: Conservation
sections.guidance: One line: assessed status and the main pressure on it, naming the assessing body.

sections.heading: Sources
sections.guidance: Deterministic.

sections.heading: Notes
sections.guidance: Owner-authored.
Deterministic.

fungus.lead_guidance: One or two sentences: what the fungus is, its family, its fruiting body, and its habit. Give the scientific name once, in italics, if the note title does not already carry it.

sections.guidance: What the fruiting body looks like, what it grows on, and its ecological habit. Never describe a fungus as edible in the lead.

sections.heading: Identification
sections.guidance: Cap shape, colour and surface; gills, pores or teeth and how they attach; stipe including any ring or volva; flesh colour and any bruising reaction; spore print colour; smell. Spore print and attachment separate more species than cap colour does.

sections.heading: Habitat & Substrate
sections.guidance: One or two lines: what it grows on or with, the trees it partners with, and its range. The host tree is often the identification.

sections.heading: Ecology
sections.guidance: Mycorrhizal, saprotrophic or parasitic, and what that means for where it appears. Name the partner species where the sources do.

sections.heading: Look-alikes
sections.guidance: Each bullet names one species confused with this one and the single feature that separates them. Say plainly where a look-alike is dangerous. This section is the reason a fungus card exists, so write it even when the sources are thin, and say what the sources do not settle.

sections.heading: Phenology

columns.guidance: One of the events named in phenology-events.json for this kind. Nothing else.

Prefer a coarse window you can support over a precise one you cannot. For a fungus the event is fruiting, and present where a perennial bracket persists.

sections.heading: Edibility & Toxicity
sections.guidance: Owner-authored. Whether to eat a mushroom is a judgment with a real cost of being wrong, made from a specimen in hand and not from an encyclopedia paragraph, so the pipeline never writes or reads this section.
